strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes an underexplored and practically relevant problem setting (Noise-Aware Generalization, NAG) that sits at the intersection of domain generalization and learning with noisy labels, and clearly articulates why naive combinations of LNL and DG methods fail.

The empirical study is extensive: 11 state-of-the-art DG/LNL methods plus 18 combinations across two real-world and two synthetic noisy datasets, providing a useful benchmark for future work on this task.

The manual annotation of noise in the VLCS dataset (Appendix A) is a valuable resource contribution, and the analysis of how LNL sample selection skews domain distributions (Sec. 5.3.1) and the quality-vs-quantity experiment (Fig. 7) offer genuine insights.
The proposed DL4ND method is simple, plug-and-play, and shows consistent relative gains (up to ~20%) across most settings, particularly under high synthetic noise.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak. 'Theorem 1' is essentially a restatement of Assumption 1 with cross-domain expectations; it is closer to a definitional condition than a proven result, and Assumption 1 itself is asserted rather than characterized. The paper would benefit from either removing the formalism or providing actual conditions under which cross-domain proxies separate noise from domain shift.

Evaluation validity concerns: the VLCS test sets were modified by removing manually identified noisy samples, which changes the benchmark and makes results hard to compare against prior DG literature on the original VLCS. The annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement are not described.

No variance, standard deviations, or significance testing are reported for any result; given the small margins in several comparisons (e.g., 0.6% and 3% differences discussed in Sec. 5.1) and the many method combinations, the reliability of individual rankings is unclear. It is also ambiguous how many seeds/runs were used.

The method has unspecified or weakly justified components: how the 'optimal label update step' is determined, sensitivity to the GMM-based loss split (which implicitly couples to the noise ratio), whether refinement is performed once or iteratively on harder datasets, and behavior when the noise is not pairwise/asymmetric.

Results are mixed and not fully explained: ERM++ + DL4ND shows ID declines on OfficeHome (Table 3, red entries), DL4ND alone is not consistently best on CHAMMI-CP, and the strongest headline result (ERM++ + DL4ND on VLCS, 95.36 ID) is conspicuously higher than every other configuration without discussion of why.

Novelty of the core technique is moderate; proxy-based relabeling via cross-domain feature comparison is a natural extension of existing similarity/confidence-based LNL ideas, and the paper does not position against closely related domain-aware noise handling (e.g., LNL+K [68], Humblot-Renaux et al. [21]) with direct experimental comparison.

Writing quality issues (typos such as 'Compairisons', 'class ad domain', 'effect in all three aspects', 'trained via ERM') and some missing details (e.g., Sec. B.2 'Synthesized Noise' is essentially empty of detail in the main supplementary text) reduce clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection problem: simultaneously handling label noise and multi-domain distribution shifts (NAG), which is practically relevant for real-world datasets like VLCS and CHAMMI-CP.

The empirical observation that noisy samples may be indistinguishable from domain-shifted samples within a single domain but separable via cross-domain comparisons is an interesting and useful insight.

The paper provides a broad empirical study (11 DG/LNL baselines, 18 combinations, 4 datasets) and offers useful analysis of why naive LNL+DG combinations fail (e.g., sample selection skewing domain distributions).
Manual noise annotation of VLCS and identification of noise in CHAMMI-CP could be a resource for the community.
The proposed method is simple and presented as plug-and-play, requiring no extra data or learning overhead.
weaknesses: The 'Theorem 1' is essentially a restatement of Assumption 1 applied to cross-domain proxies; it is not a proven result about any real featurizer and thus provides little theoretical support. The formal framing overstates the contribution.

The core method (DL4ND) is a fairly heuristic one-shot relabeling pipeline (GMM loss splitting + (class, domain) proxy averaging + nearest-proxy relabeling). Novelty is limited relative to existing low-loss selection and proxy/prototype-based LNL methods, and there is no ablation isolating the contributions of the GMM split, proxy construction, or cross-domain averaging.

Key methodological details are underspecified: how the 'optimal label update step' is determined, sensitivity to the number of relabeling rounds, behavior when a domain has few low-loss samples for a class, and how the method handles multi-label or ambiguous samples (relevant to VLCS, which the paper itself notes has multi-object images).

The evaluation is on only two real-world datasets (one of which, VLCS, is small), plus synthetic noise experiments. Many results show modest gains (often <1-2 points) with no error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, making the claimed improvements difficult to assess. The 'up to 20% relative gain' claim relies on the toy RotatedMNIST experiment, which is not representative.

There are concerning inconsistencies and weak points in the empirical story: DL4ND used standalone (group c) beats many sophisticated LNL baselines with almost no discussion of how; some DL4ND+DG combinations (e.g., MIRO+DL4ND, ERM+++DL4ND on CHAMMI-CP) underperform their base methods and are not analyzed; the VLCS test set is modified by removing annotated noisy samples, complicating comparison with prior published results.

Assumption 1 (class structure dominates domain structure in feature space) may not hold for many real DG settings (e.g., PACS, TerraIncognita), and the paper does not test when the assumption fails or provide any diagnostic; the method's failure modes are unexplored.

The NAG task formulation inherits domain labels during training, which many DG works consider unrealistic; the paper's own Fig. 2 frames domain-aware methods as a separate branch, yet the main method depends on domain labels without justifying this assumption.

Writing and presentation issues: typos ('Compairisons', 'class ad domain', 'effect in all three aspects'), unclear text (e.g., the confusing numeric comparison in Sec. 3.2.1), Fig. 3 caption/axis details, and formatting problems in Tables 1 and 3 reduce clarity and polish.
Reproducibility is limited: hyperparameters for DL4ND (loss thresholding, GMM parameters, number of proxies) are not reported, and code is only promised upon acceptance.

Missing related baselines: the method is essentially a noise-filtering + relabeling scheme, but no comparison against general robust training/relabelling baselines adapted to multi-domain settings is provided.

strengths: The paper identifies an underexplored and practically relevant problem at the intersection of domain generalization and learning with noisy labels (NAG), with a clear motivation and good illustrations of why existing LNL assumptions break under domain shifts.

The empirical study is broad: 11 DG/LNL methods, 18 combination methods, four datasets, including valuable new noise annotations of real-world benchmarks (VLCS, CHAMMI-CP) and controlled synthetic noise experiments across multiple noise ratios.

The analysis of why naive LNL+DG combinations fail (sample selection skewing domain distributions, domain shift confusing noise detection) provides genuine insight for the community, supported by concrete evidence (e.g., Fig. 7).
The proposed DL4ND is simple, plug-and-play, and yields consistent gains in many settings, with strong relative improvements in high-noise regimes (up to ~20%).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: DL4ND essentially combines a GMM-based low/high-loss split (as in DivideMix-style methods) with nearest-proxy relabeling. The cross-domain averaging trick is intuitive but a small delta over existing label-correction techniques; no comparison against stronger label-correction baselines adapted to the multi-domain setting.

The theoretical contribution is weak: Theorem 1 is essentially a restatement of Assumption 1 and is not proven or empirically validated in a rigorous sense; the separability condition is an assumption, not a result.

Evaluation concerns: the VLCS test sets were modified by removing manually identified noisy samples, hurting comparability with prior published results; no error bars, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported despite many small differences (e.g., 0.6-3% gaps) used to support claims.

Key method details are underspecified or fragile: when the 'optimal label update step' occurs, sensitivity to the number of label refinement rounds, behavior when the low-loss proxy set is itself contaminated, and failure cases of relabeling (e.g., class-imbalance amplification) are not analyzed.

Mixed results are under-discussed: on CHAMMI-CP some DL4ND combinations decline (e.g., ERM++ + DL4ND), and gains on some settings are marginal; the paper's claims of 'significant improvement' are stronger than the evidence in some cells of Table 2/3.

Writing quality issues: typos (e.g., 'Compairisons', 'class ad domain'), garbled caption in Fig. 2 ('DG typically methods either ignore... or both (e.g., same citations)'), and incomplete Appendix B.2 (synthesized noise section is empty), which hurts reproducibility and polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored intersection of Learning with Noisy Labels (LNL) and Domain Generalization (DG), formalized as Noise-Aware Generalization (NAG), and convincingly argues why this setting poses challenges that do not appear in either task alone.

The preliminary analysis (Figures 1, 4; Equation 2; SVM support-vector analysis) provides valuable insight into why noise and domain shifts are hard to separate, and why cross-domain comparisons help — this gives the method a principled motivation rather than being purely heuristic.
The proposed DL4ND is simple, requires no additional data or learned components beyond a GMM, and is compatible with existing DG methods, making it broadly applicable.

The evaluation is extensive: 7 datasets (real and synthetic noise), 12 DG/LNL baselines, ~20 DG+LNL combinations, component ablations (Table 5), relabeling precision analysis (Table 6), warmup sensitivity (Tables 12-13), and a thoughtful analysis of why naive UNICON+DG combinations fail due to domain-distribution skew (Figure 7, Table 7).
Code release and a reproducibility statement support reproducibility; implementation details and integration algorithms for all baselines are provided.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest. DL4ND essentially combines well-known ingredients — small-loss sample selection, GMM loss-thresholding (as in UNICON), and nearest-prototype relabeling — with the main addition being cross-domain proxy comparisons. The strongest justification for acceptance is the empirical study and analysis rather than the method itself.

Gains on real-world noise benchmarks are often small (e.g., 1-2% on VLCS and PACS over strong DG baselines like SAGM+SWAD), while the headline 12.5% gains come from high-noise synthetic settings (e.g., 60% symmetric noise on OfficeHome). Real-world impact claims could be overinterpreted.

The method relies on the availability of domain labels at training time, which simplifies the NAG problem relative to the fully unsupervised case; while acknowledged, no experiments relax this assumption.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing appear to be reported for the main comparisons, despite some reported margins being within 1-2%. This weakens the evidence for several claims (e.g., DL4ND vs. ELR on CHAMMI-CP).

The method assumes noise is detectable via feature-space proximity and that a sufficient pool of clean low-loss samples exists; there is limited analysis of failure modes (e.g., severe instance-dependent noise, rare classes, or highly overlapping class semantics), and no experiments varying the number of source domains.

Writing quality issues remain (typos such as 'booting performance', 'ride range', 'IMPELMENTATION DETAILS', 'provide into deeper insights'), and Figure 6's relative-change plots make absolute performance levels hard to assess without consulting the appendix.
Warmup length requires a validation set for tuning and its sensitivity varies across datasets (Tables 12-13), adding an extra tuning burden not fully characterized.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and relatively underexplored intersection of learning with noisy labels (LNL) and domain generalization (DG), and the framing of 'Noise-Aware Generalization' (NAG) is clearly motivated.

The diagnostic analysis (Section 3, Figures 1 and 4) provides useful insight into why naive LNL-style noise detection fails when domain shifts are present, and the SVM support-vector analysis (Section 3.2) gives a concrete motivation for why ambiguous samples matter.

Breadth of evaluation is commendable: 12 prior DG/LNL methods, 20 combinations, 7 datasets spanning real and synthetic noise, plus ablations, relabeling-precision analysis, warmup sensitivity, and per-domain sampling comparisons.
The analysis in Section 5.2 (UNICON skewing domain distributions, Figure 7) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding that explains why naive LNL+DG combinations fail.

The paper appears reproducible in principle: a unified codebase, implementation details, pretrained models, and detailed noise specifications are promised, and baseline descriptions and integration algorithms are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. DL4ND is essentially standard small-loss sample selection (well-established since Co-teaching/early-learning work) combined with (class, domain) proxies and nearest-proxy relabeling. This is an intuitive engineering combination rather than a new technique; the relation to UNICON is acknowledged but the delta is modest.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The abstract states DL4ND 'outperforms DG and LNL methods,' yet in Table 8 DL4ND alone (88.6 AVG on VLCS) loses to SAGM+SWAD (89.5); DL4ND is only competitive when combined with DG methods. Gains on real-world noise are often modest (1-2%), and several results are mixed (e.g., in Table 2, ERM++ w/ DL4ND decreases ID accuracy; in Table 4, w/ DL4ND underperforms SAGM on TerraIncognita 20% noise).

Heavy reliance on assumptions that weaken generality: the method requires domain labels, assumes the loss distribution is cleanly bimodal (GMM with two clusters), assumes low-loss samples are clean, and requires that cross-domain features be comparable - assumptions that may fail for datasets with few domains, many classes, or severe instance-dependent noise. No theoretical or formal justification for Equation (2) is provided beyond empirical observation.

Inconsistencies and presentation problems undermine confidence: Table 4 has missing entries for the no-noise condition; Table 1's jump in label accuracy from 75.7 to 98.1 (with 30% asymmetric noise) is surprising and under-analyzed; there are numerous typos and grammatical errors ('IMPELMENTATION', 'booting performance', 'ride range', 'provide into deeper insights', 'additionl'), and the code footnote is empty ('Code:').

The headline 'gains up to 12.5%' is driven by the most extreme synthetic setting (60% symmetric noise on OfficeHome with a weak ERM baseline), which is not representative of the typical improvement; average gains on real-world noise datasets are substantially smaller.

Positioning against the closest related area (DA+LNL methods) is relegated to an appendix, and the argument that DA+LNL methods are 'well represented in the LNL literature' is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated; several DA+LNL methods are argued away rather than adapted and compared.

Scope of the 'NAG' contribution is unclear: prior work (Qiao & Low 2024; Seo et al. 2020) already benchmarked DG under label noise, so the primary novelty is the proposed method, which as noted is incremental. The significance of the contribution for a top-tier venue is thus limited.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes an underexplored and practically relevant problem: Noise-Aware Generalization (NAG), where models must be robust to both label noise and domain shifts. The framing (Figure 2) clearly distinguishes NAG from DG, LNL, and their naive combinations.

The core observation — that noisy samples indistinguishable within a domain become separable via cross-domain comparisons using low-loss proxies — is intuitive, well motivated by the analysis in Section 3 (Figure 4, the SVM support vector experiment in Section 3.2), and leads to a simple, practical method (DL4ND) requiring no extra data or learning overhead.

Evaluation is broad and thorough: 7 datasets (3 real-noise including a biomedical dataset, 4 synthetic), 12 DG/LNL baselines plus 20 combinations, controlled symmetric/asymmetric noise experiments, component ablations (Table 5), relabeling precision analysis (Table 6), warmup sensitivity (Tables 12-13), and detailed noise statistics for VLCS (Table 14).

The analysis in Section 5.2 on WHY naive LNL+DG combinations fail (LNL selection skews domain distributions, Figure 7; per-domain sampling ablation in Table 7) provides genuine insight beyond simply reporting numbers, and is valuable for future NAG research.
Reproducibility appears strong: unified codebase released, implementation details and integration algorithms (Appendix D) provided, pretrained models included.
weaknesses: The method assumes access to domain labels, which substantially simplifies the problem and limits applicability. While the paper acknowledges this and argues it 'simplifies' rather than solves NAG, the practical scenarios where domain labels are available but labels are noisy deserve more discussion.

The technical contribution of DL4ND is relatively simple: GMM loss-based sample splitting plus nearest-proxy relabeling across domains. It is an incremental extension of existing LNL relabeling ideas (e.g., UNICON, DivideMix) with the cross-domain twist; the novelty is more in the problem insight than the method itself.

Gains on real-world noise datasets are modest (1-2% average on VLCS, CHAMMI-CP, PACS), with the headline 12.5% figure coming from a controlled symmetric-noise setting. Some results are mixed — e.g., DL4ND degrades ID performance in several OfficeHome/TerraIncognita settings (Table 4) — and inconsistent gains across DG+DL4ND combinations (ERM++ best with DL4ND but MIRO+SWAD not) suggest fragility.
Reliability of results is unclear: no error bars, standard deviations, or number of seeds/runs are reported for the main tables, which matters given the small margins on real-noise datasets.

The definition of 'real-world noise' in VLCS/PACS is essentially missing multi-label annotations (unlabeled categories per Table 14) treated as single-label noise; treating these as label noise is a somewhat debatable modeling choice that affects comparability with prior DG work.

Writing has several errors and unclear passages (e.g., 'IMPELMENTATION', 'ride range of applications', 'booting performance', Equation 2 notation with hat placement is hard to parse), and some experimental setup details (e.g., how ID accuracy is computed in the leave-one-out protocol) could be clearer.
